item.title: Minimum wage board meeting delay raises concern
item.description:
The third meeting of the Minimum Wage Board, where garment factory owners were scheduled to submit their proposals for the new minimum wage structure for readymade garment (RMG) workers, was abruptly postponed on Monday morning (November 16).
Despite owners having completed their preparations in advance to submit the proposal, Board Secretary Raisa Afroz issued an official notice Monday morning announcing that the 11:00 AM meeting at the Department of Labour had been postponed due to "unavoidable circumstances" upon instructions from the authorities.
Speaking to reporters regarding the sudden suspension, Minimum Wage Board chairman Syed Azad Subhani stated: "One of our permanent board members suddenly fell ill and had to be admitted to the hospital. It would not be appropriate to hold the board meeting without him. That is why we have postponed it. The new date for the next meeting will be announced shortly."
Following the postponement, the apex trade bodies of the apparel sector—the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA)—issued a joint press release signed by BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan and BKMEA President Mohammad Hatem.
The two organizations stated that the owners' side was fully prepared to present its wage proposal at Monday's meeting.
Pointing out that the new wage structure is scheduled to come into effect on December 1, they noted that timely completion of the board's activities would allow factories the necessary time to prepare for paying increased wages.
Accordingly, the trade bodies urged the authorities to announce a new date for the postponed meeting as soon as possible.
Meanwhile, Taslima Akhter, president of the Bangladesh Garment Sramik Samhati, told Dhaka Tribune: "We have heard that the meeting was postponed because a board member fell ill. We want the owners' proposal to be accepted within the stipulated timeframe so that wage-fixing discussions can move forward. To finalize and implement the new pay structure, the board must convene quickly.”
Garment workers have been protesting since last month demanding a wage hike. In response, the government formed a new Minimum Wage Board on November 1.
At the board's first meeting on November 4, it was announced that the new wage structure would take effect from December 1.
During the second meeting on November 9, workers' representative Babul Akhter proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk32,000.
As the owners' side was unable to present its proposal on that day, they were granted four working days, which led up to Monday's scheduled session.
Previously, the last minimum wage for garment workers was announced in November 2023, raising the minimum monthly pay from Tk8,000 to Tk12,500.

item.title: Shama: India’s reported conditions for Hasina’s return have no legal basis
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam has dismissed reports that India has set conditions for the return of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, saying the reported demands have no basis in Bangladesh's laws.
Responding to reports that India had sought to ensure Hasina's right to appeal and restart her trial before agreeing to her return, Shama said Bangladesh had received no such proposal.
“No, not at all. We have had no such conversations with them on this matter,” she told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, referring to reports published by BBC Bangla.
She said Bangladesh expects Hasina, who has been sentenced to death for crimes against humanity, to be brought back from India under the existing extradition treaty.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has written to India multiple times under the extradition treaty,” she said, adding that the Ministries of Law and Home Affairs are examining the legal and technical aspects of the matter.
Shama said the government believes Hasina, like any other accused person, should be returned under the treaty to serve her sentence.
She also questioned whether Hasina's Bangladeshi citizenship alone would guarantee her the right to obtain a passport, saying the relevant laws do not require the government to issue passports to convicted criminals or individuals facing serious cases.
On bilateral relations, Shama said Bangladesh-India ties extend far beyond the issue of Hasina, emphasizing the longstanding relationship between the 2 neighboring countries and the importance of addressing bilateral matters through diplomacy.
“Bangladesh-India relations are a much bigger deal than Sheikh Hasina,” she said, urging against giving the issue more importance than necessary.
“We have issues. We will deal with the issues through diplomacy,” she said.
However, Shama said the government could not ignore Hasina's activities in India if they were aimed at destabilizing Bangladesh.
Regarding the Bangladesh-India Consular Dialogue, originally scheduled for November 17-18, Shama said the meeting had not been cancelled but deferred until a mutually convenient time.
She described reports of its cancellation as misinformation, saying both sides had agreed that it would be better to hold the talks later when they were available.
The state minister also indicated that Bangladesh would host several high-level foreign visits in the coming days, although she did not disclose any names or tentative dates.
Asked whether water-sharing issues, particularly the Ganges water issue, had been discussed at a meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Shama said the government could hold extensive discussions with the prime minister on a range of issues.
However, she did not directly confirm whether the Ganges water issue had been discussed at the meeting.

item.title: How late HIV detection claimed a 27-year-old in Bangladesh
item.description:
His mother clung to her son’s body as it lay on a stretcher in the intensive care unit of Dhaka’s Infectious Diseases Hospital in Mohakhali, crying inconsolably, as though letting go of him would mean accepting that he was never coming home.
He was just 27.
A former student of two of Bangladesh’s most respected educational institutions, Tayeeb (pseudonym) had completed his master’s degree about two years earlier and was looking for a job, with the prospect of a professional life still ahead of him.
His family was financially comfortable, and he had the support and opportunities that many young people could only hope for.
Yet none of these could protect him from an infection that, until he became critically ill, his family did not even know he had.
Tayeeb died on Monday after being diagnosed with HIV and cryptococcal meningitis, a potentially life-threatening fungal infection that affects the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord, according to doctors at the hospital.
For his family, the diagnosis was devastating.
They had never known he was living with HIV, and by the time the infection was discovered, his condition had already deteriorated severely.
According to his uncle, Tayeeb initially sought treatment at a private hospital after developing a persistent headache.
Medical examinations revealed a fungal infection in his brain and an HIV infection, following which he was referred to the Infectious Diseases Hospital.
His uncle said the family learned of the HIV diagnosis on October 15.
They had no clear idea how he had contracted the virus; although the family reported no known history of blood transfusion, they could not identify a likely route of transmission.
Doctors told the family that the infection had reached an advanced stage, his uncle said.
Tayeeb’s story challenges the assumption that HIV is a problem confined to people living in poverty or without access to education and resources.
He came from a financially comfortable family and had studied at some of the country’s leading institutions, yet the infection remained undetected until serious complications had developed.
At the Infectious Diseases Hospital, his final days unfolded amid a heavy burden of HIV patients.
Superintendent Dr FA Asma Khan told this correspondent that 24 people living with HIV were admitted to the hospital on the same day, against its capacity of 25 beds for such patients.
More than 2,000 people were enrolled on the hospital’s HIV services to receive medication, she said.
“Today, we have 19 measles patients and 24 HIV patients,” Khan said.
The hospital figures offer a snapshot of the pressure on one of Bangladesh’s key public facilities for infectious diseases, as the country records a sharp rise in newly detected HIV infections.
The National HIV/AIDS Situation Report 2025 recorded 1,891 new HIV cases between November 2024 and October 2025, up from 1,438 in the preceding 12-month period, an increase of about 31.5%.
It also recorded 254 HIV/AIDS-related deaths during the period, compared with 326 a year earlier.
An estimated 17,480 people were living with HIV in Bangladesh in 2025.
But the challenge extends beyond diagnosis and access to medication.
For many people living with HIV, stigma and discrimination remain formidable obstacles to seeking treatment and living a normal life.
A health worker involved in a Global Fund-supported project to control HIV in Bangladesh said many of the patients encountered by their team were men, including men who have sex with men (MSM) and bisexual men.
Many were also strikingly young, often just 22 or 23 years old, including university students, the worker said.
At an age when they should be pursuing their studies, building careers and making plans for the future, these young men are instead having to navigate an HIV diagnosis alongside the fear of rejection and social discrimination.
The worker stressed that people who take antiretroviral medication regularly can live healthy, normal lives.
The greater obstacles, in many cases, are a lack of awareness, fear and the social taboos surrounding the virus.
The worker also described instances in which doctors had allegedly refused to perform surgery on people living with HIV out of fear that other patients might become infected, a misconception that can deny patients essential medical care.
An infectious disease specialist who works closely with people living with HIV said such fears were medically unfounded, explaining that HIV does not spread through ordinary contact between patients and that standard infection-control measures and proper sterilisation procedures are sufficient to prevent transmission in healthcare settings.
A person's HIV status alone is not a reason to deny them surgery.
Doctors say HIV can remain undetected for years, allowing the virus to progressively weaken the immune system without the person knowing they are infected.
By the time symptoms become severe, patients may already be vulnerable to infections, illnesses that a healthy immune system would ordinarily be able to fight off.
Cryptococcal meningitis is one such infection, and earlier HIV diagnosis can allow appropriate care to begin before such life-threatening complications develop.
For Tayeeb’s family, however, the questions remain unanswered: when he contracted the virus, how long he had been living with it, and whether he had any indication of his condition before he became seriously ill.
His uncle said the family has been searching for an answer ever since.
“We asked his friends. The counsellors asked him, and the doctor asked him separately. He could not tell us how it happened, and he could not even imagine it,” the uncle said.
“We went through the reasons one by one, three or four of them. The first was sexual transmission. But no, he is a man of prayer. He reads the Quran. He does not even smoke. Then we thought maybe it was drugs or injections. But his friends come to our house, and they call me mama. They told us that when he had to get an injection, he would take one of them along with him, because he was so afraid of needles. How could he take drugs?”
“Then we asked about blood. But he never needed a transfusion. Whether he gave blood to someone while he was at university, I do not know,”
“It is simply a misfortune,” the uncle said.
He had studied, graduated and was looking for a beginning.
However, he never got the chance because of HIV.
His death is a reminder that timely testing can be critical to preventing a manageable infection from progressing into a life-threatening illness.

item.title: Dengue death toll crosses 500 as three die in 24hrs
item.description:
Three more people died from dengue and 1,598 were hospitalized with the mosquito-borne disease in the 24 hours till 8am Monday, taking the country's death toll to 502 this year.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), a total of 164,107 dengue patients have been hospitalized across the country so far this year.
Of the newly hospitalized patients, 673 were in Dhaka Division, 61 in Mymensingh Division, 251 in Chattogram Division, 201 in Khulna Division, 145 in Rajshahi Division, 71 in Rangpur Division, 185 in Barisal Division and 11 in Sylhet Division.
Meanwhile, 157,988 dengue patients have recovered and returned home after receiving treatment in hospitals.
Last year, a total of 102,861 people were infected with dengue, while 413 died from the mosquito-borne disease.

item.title: Bangladesh’s childcare crisis is holding women back from work
item.description:
Four in every 10 mothers in urban Bangladesh who are not employed say childcare responsibilities are a major reason they cannot enter the workforce, exposing how the lack of affordable and accessible daycare is limiting women’s economic participation.
According to a policy brief titled “Childcare in Bangladesh: What Families Need, What Providers Deliver, and Where the Gaps Remain,” published by the World Bank’s South Asia Gender Innovation Lab, 38.4% of non-working mothers in urban areas identified childcare responsibilities as a key barrier to taking up employment.
The findings point to a significant gap between Bangladesh’s ambition to increase women’s participation in the economy and the everyday challenges faced by mothers who cannot find reliable care for their children.
The problem is particularly concerning amid a large population of young people who are neither in education, employment nor training (NEET). Around 9.6 million people aged 15-29 fall into this category in Bangladesh, with women accounting for approximately two-thirds of the total.
The World Bank’s research draws on demand-side surveys involving 1,700 respondents in rural and semi-urban areas and nearly 3,000 mothers in urban industrial areas. It also maps 514 childcare providers in Dhaka and examines the operations of 335 of them.
The scale of the challenge is particularly evident in Dhaka, where more than 21 million people have access to only 514 identified childcare providers, including government, private, non-profit, madrasa-based and home-based facilities.
The average capacity of the surveyed centers was just 55 children, indicating a substantial mismatch between the availability of childcare services and the needs of families in the capital.
The study found that 57% of government childcare centers had waiting lists, limiting access to some of the most affordable formal services.
Only 0.1% of mothers in urban areas reported using institutional daycare facilities, while around 20% relied on home-based childcare providers.
The findings also highlight the financial barriers facing families. Around 61% of urban mothers reported having no formal or family-based support for childcare. Among these mothers, 87% said they could not afford paid childcare services.
Private commercial daycare centers are largely concentrated in higher-income neighborhoods, while low- and lower-middle-income families have fewer affordable options.
The study suggests that the availability of childcare alone is not enough. Parents also consider distance, affordability and trust when deciding where to leave their children.
Mothers in semi-urban areas were willing to pay an additional Tk1,000-1,700 per month for childcare facilities closer to their homes rather than near their workplaces or training centers.
They were also willing to pay up to Tk1,200 more per month to leave their children with a familiar and trusted caregiver rather than an unfamiliar professional provider.
These preferences indicate that families often priorities convenient locations and trusted caregivers over conventional institutional arrangements.
The World Bank’s assessment notes that families want childcare services that are affordable, close to home, trustworthy and supportive of children’s development. However, existing formal services remain limited, unevenly distributed and beyond the financial reach of many low-income households.
Bangladesh enacted the Child Daycare Centre Act in 2021, providing for registration, inspections and penalties for violations. However, significant gaps remain in translating the legal framework into accessible and quality childcare services.
The World Bank’s Women, Business and the Law 2026 report gives Bangladesh a score of zero out of 100 on the relevant supportive-framework indicators, highlighting the lack of the necessary institutional arrangements and policy support to make childcare provisions effective in practice.
The study also identifies substantial differences in service quality between formal and informal providers.
Government-run centers generally perform better in terms of trained staff, physical safety and food arrangements. However, their limited availability and waiting lists restrict access.
By contrast, none of the surveyed home-based childcare providers had received formal training, while many lacked basic safety equipment.
The World Bank’s Early Learning Partnership framework identifies seven essential elements of quality childcare: trained caregivers, warm and responsive interactions, safe and healthy environments, appropriate caregiver-to-child ratios, structured daily routines, play-based learning and regular engagement with parents.
Beyond the shortage of childcare facilities, social attitudes and household decision-making also influence women’s ability to work.
Surveys in rural and semi-urban areas found that majorities of both men and women supported women’s participation in economic activities. However, opposition within families, particularly from male members, remained a significant obstacle.
Around 90% of wives surveyed supported women’s income-earning activities, compared with approximately 67% of husbands.
The findings suggest that expanding childcare facilities must go hand in hand with efforts to change social attitudes and encourage men to share responsibility for childcare and household work.
The World Bank research highlights the importance of social and behavioral change (SBC) initiatives targeting men and families to strengthen support for women’s economic participation.
The World Bank argues that expanding large institutional daycare centers through public funding alone may not be sufficient to address the country’s childcare gap.
Instead, it recommends recognizing and improving home-based childcare services, particularly in densely populated and low-income communities.
One initiative is the Recovery and Advancement of Informal Sector Employment (RAISE) project, jointly supported by the World Bank and the Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF). Under the initiative, women in densely populated areas receive training and financial support to establish childcare micro-enterprises.
The study also calls for a more flexible regulatory approach. Excessively punitive requirements and bureaucratic procedures could force small informal providers to close, further reducing childcare options for low-income families.
Instead, inspections should be accompanied by training, first-aid kits, childproofing materials and practical guidance to improve safety and service quality.
Other priorities include targeted subsidies to make childcare affordable for low-income households and revisions to the 2021 law to provide appropriate legal recognition and protection for different childcare models, including public, private and home-based services.
The findings underline that childcare is not simply a family or social welfare issue. It is also an economic concern that directly affects women’s ability to earn, build careers and contribute to national growth.
Without affordable, accessible and reliable childcare, a significant proportion of Bangladesh’s potential female workforce may continue to remain outside the labor market.

item.title: Information Commission resumes RTI complaint hearings after nearly two years
item.description:
The Information Commission Bangladesh has resumed hearing complaints filed under the Right to Information (RTI) Act after nearly two years.
The Commission held hearings on five complaints on Monday, disposing of three of them and fixing dates for further hearings on the remaining two.
Chief Information Commissioner Prof Dr Nahreen Islam Khan, along with Information Commissioners S A M Mahfuzur Rahman and Khan Mohammad Abul Hossain, conducted the hearings.
With the Commission remaining non-functional for an extended period, a total of 917 complaints were filed over the past two years. The government reconstituted the Information Commission on October 17.
After assuming office, the newly constituted Commission adopted a 100-day action plan, prioritizing the disposal of pending complaints. As part of the initiative, it is working to expedite the hearing and resolution process.
The complaints heard on Monday concerned the non-disclosure of information relating to recruitment by various public and private institutions, land ownership and income-expenditure accounts of institutions, development projects and allocations of local government bodies, reasons for cancellation of appointment letters, recruitment examination answer scripts, and the leasing of government property.

item.title: EC to hold first-phase UP elections in 1,026 unions on Jan 21
item.description:
The Election Commission (EC) will hold elections to 1,026 Union Parishads (UPs) under 131 upazilas in the first phase on January 21.
The decision was taken at an EC meeting held at the Nirbachan Bhaban in the city's Agargaon area on Monday.
After the meeting, Election Commissioner Abul Fazal Md Sanaullah briefed journalists on the decisions.
The EC has planned to arrange elections to more than 4000 UPs in the five-phase election in the early next year.
The lists of UPs for each phase election will be published on the EC website by next Thursday, said the Election Commissioner.
According to the plan, elections in the second phase will be held in 1,113 UPs under 129 upazilas, the third phase in 1,002 UPs under 118 upazilas, the fourth phase in 793 UPs under 93 upazilas and the fifth phase in 356 UPs under 37 upazilas.
The Election Commission has also planned to hold discussions with political parties ahead of the UP elections and complete the dialogue by December 10.
Abul Fazl said the matter was discussed at Monday's meeting and the commission plans to invite registered political parties for discussions over three days, either late this month or early December, following their registration serial numbers.
Asked whether any political party had demanded the deployment of army personnel in local government elections, he said the commission had not received any such demand so far.
The commission would take necessary measures after assessing whether the agencies concerned could effectively perform their duties in particular areas and maintain the election environment, he added.
The meeting also discussed ongoing problems with National Identity Card (NID) services and smart card printing.
Abul Fazl said the software used for smart card printing had been experiencing problems over the last four to five days. However, he claimed that no NID services had been suspended due to the problem and said efforts were underway to resolve it.
The commission also decided that Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) would no longer be used in any election.
The meeting reviewed progress made by a committee formed to determine how the EVMs currently in storage would be disposed of.
Abul Fazl said the commission had received an update on the committee's progress.
Asked about environmental concerns and financial losses associated with destroying the EVMs, he said these issues had not yet been discussed by the commission.

item.title: ‘Taste of America’ in Dhaka: Ambassador pushes for wider US food access
item.description:
The US embassy in Dhaka organized a day-long food and agricultural products exhibition, “Taste of America”, at the Sheraton Hotel in Banani on Monday to mark 250 years of US independence and promote agricultural trade between Bangladesh and the United States.
Speaking as the chief guest at the opening session, US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T Christensen said reducing trade barriers would allow consumers in Bangladesh to access a wider variety of products at lower prices.
The exhibition showcased agricultural products, food items and culinary ingredients, including premium US beef. It aimed to highlight the quality and commercial potential of American food products to Bangladeshi importers, chefs, restaurants and businesses in the hospitality sector.
The ambassador said facilitating the entry of more US products into Bangladesh was one of his key priorities. Expanding trade would give American companies access to new markets while enabling Bangladeshi businesses to import high-quality products and ingredients, benefiting both economies.
He said import costs would decrease once the trade agreement between the 2 countries came into effect, as reduced tariffs would make American food imports easier and more affordable.
On food safety, he said products must pass prescribed tests before they can be exported to the US market. He added that the trade agreement emphasized high standards of food safety, intellectual property protection and an effective regulatory system.
Highlighting the market situation in Bangladesh, Christensen said import restrictions and an unregulated market system drove up the prices of many products. Counterfeit and adulterated food products also forced consumers to spend more while creating uncertainty about quality.
“Every family has the right to safe and quality food at fair prices,” he said, adding that initiatives to gradually reduce trade barriers would continue.
The ambassador said American beef, known internationally for steaks, also had commercial potential alongside traditional Bangladeshi dishes such as biryani, polao, mezban and tehari.
He said grain-based feeding produced distinctive marbling, tenderness and flavor, while the US Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Choice and Prime grades were internationally recognized as high-quality products.
He said there was currently no opportunity to legally purchase American beef in Bangladesh, meaning those seeking premium American steak had to travel to Bangkok, Singapore, Tokyo or the United States.

The US embassy would work with the Bangladesh government to ensure commercial access to premium US beef in the country, he added.
Christensen also said that following the approval of tariff concessions in 2025, Bangladesh had become the ninth-largest buyer of US wheat. He called on the country to import more wheat, process it locally and use it in restaurants and cafes.
Halal-slaughtered beef imported from Iowa, the ambassador's home state, was served to guests at the event.
The exhibition also featured a cupcake-making competition in which Bangladeshi bakers used American ingredients. Business networking sessions brought together importers, chefs, restaurants and hospitality businesses, while live music performances were also held.

item.title: PM urges students to help keep Dhaka clean, protect environment
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday emphasized the role of students in keeping Dhaka clean and protecting the environment, encouraging them to plant more trees, care for animals and wildlife, and develop skills and a sense of social responsibility to become worthy citizens of the country.
“Give trees as gifts to your loved ones on their birthdays. Planting more trees will improve the environment. You may think, ‘what do I gain if the environment improves?’ We all will benefit,” he said.
The prime minister made the remarks when he met students, who had come to visit the National Parliament and watch its proceedings, during the Maghrib prayer break in the evening.
Tarique also stressed the importance of sports and caring for animals and other living creatures, saying human beings were the best of creation and had a responsibility to protect nature and wildlife.
He said students should develop skills and a sense of social responsibility to prepare themselves to become capable citizens who could contribute to the country and society.
The Prime Minister also underlined the need for vocational education, sports and language learning alongside academic studies.
Addressing the students, he said the government was introducing vocational education in schools and colleges, which would be compulsory from Class IX.
“Everyone must be properly prepared for the future. We are introducing vocational education in schools and colleges. Students will have to take vocational education compulsorily from Class IX,” Tarique said.
He also said students should take part in the Notun Kuri Sports program, which would offer six to seven different sports disciplines, allowing them to choose according to their interests.
He said sports should receive equal importance alongside academic studies.
The Prime Minister also spoke about plans to develop students' proficiency in multiple languages, saying everyone should learn an additional language apart from their mother tongue.
Students would be able to choose their preferred language from six to seven options, including English, Mandarin and Japanese, he said.
Earlier, 43 students who secured GPA-5 in the SSC examinations and six teachers from five educational institutions in Dohar upazila in Dhaka, 15 Class XII students and four teachers from the capital's Monipur High School, and nine students from Chandpur Medical College visited the National Parliament and observed parliamentary proceedings.
As part of the visit, they attended a briefing, visited the parliament library and took photographs at the North Plaza of the National Parliament.

item.title: Law and order returns to normal in Gopalganj amid intensified joint patrols
item.description:
The law and order situation in Gopalganj has returned to normal following a period of violence and unrest.
With Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel deployed and joint forces intensifying patrols, government and private offices, courts and shops across the district reopened on Monday morning. Traffic movement also returned to normal on the Dhaka-Khulna highway and roads within the district town.
Additional police and BGB personnel remain deployed at key locations across the town to prevent further incidents, while joint force patrols continue.
On Sunday, the district witnessed protests, arson and vandalism. Leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned, and its affiliated organisations have been accused of orchestrating the violence.
During the unrest, the homes of several BNP leaders were vandalised, and a Grameen Bank branch was set on fire. BGB personnel were subsequently deployed to bring the situation under control.
Meanwhile, amid the developments, the officers-in-charge (OCs) of three police stations in the district were transferred on Sunday night.
The officers are Ayub Ali of Tungipara Police Station, Riad Mahmud of Kotalipara Police Station and Mahfuzur Rahman of Kashiani Police Station. All three have been transferred to Kishoreganj district.

item.title: Khasru: IMF loan talks to conclude by Jan-Feb’27
item.description:
Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury on Sunday said discussions with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on its new loan program are expected to conclude by January-February next year.
The government has no plan to withdraw from the IMF’s new loan program, but it is working to align the lender’s conditions and program with the country’s current economic realities and the government’s own five-year development plan, he said.
“Two working groups, one from each side, are working to resolve the differences with the IMF. The necessary adjustments will be made through discussions, after which the loan program will proceed in its normal course,” the minister said.
Khasru made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after inaugurating the two-day ‘International Debt Conference Bangladesh 2026’ at Hotel Ocean Paradise in Cox’s Bazar.
Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Investment and Capital Market Tanvir Shahriar Ghani, Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Mozumder, Financial Institutions Division Secretary Nazma Mobarek and senior officials of the Finance Ministry were present.
The finance minister said the government had no intention of ending its relationship with the IMF or discontinuing the loan program. Rather, it wants to implement the program in a manner consistent with the country’s economic realities, public interests and development priorities.
He said the agreement on the existing IMF loan program was reached during the tenure of the previous unelected government. The conditions agreed upon at that time could not be implemented overnight by the present elected government.
Sudden implementation of those conditions could put additional pressure on ordinary people and adversely affect businesses, trade and the overall economy, he added.
The government, therefore, wants to ensure adequate time and a gradual approach to implementing the IMF conditions, the minister said.
He noted that the government had already aligned its development plans with those of the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (Jica).
Similar discussions are now underway to bring the IMF program in line with the government’s priorities and plans.
The minister said a lack of coordination among development partners could create complications in project implementation. The government wants to advance their programs by taking into account the country’s priorities, institutional capacity and prevailing economic conditions.
He reiterated that the government’s position on continuing the IMF loan program was clear, although it was seeking necessary adjustments to the conditions in line with the country’s circumstances.
The two working groups are continuing discussions, and the government expects to complete the negotiations and coordination process by January-February next year. The program is expected to resume its normal pace following the completion of the discussions, he said.

item.title: Garment factories in Savar, Ashulia return to normal operations
item.description:
Garment factories in Savar and Ashulia have maintained normal production following several days of tension, with most workers returning to work peacefully on Monday morning.
A visit to different industrial areas in the morning found workers entering factories within their scheduled hours.
However, law enforcement agencies remained on alert to prevent any untoward incidents. Additional police and members of other forces were deployed at key points and in front of factories.
Despite the overall improvement, production remained suspended at several factories in Ashulia.
Industrial police said more than 30 factories across the industrial zone remained closed due to labour unrest, while workers at two factories were observing work stoppages. All other factories remained open.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police of Industrial Police-1, said the situation in Savar, Ashulia and Dhamrai under his jurisdiction was normal, with operations running smoothly.
"Factory owners have kept around 30 factories closed for various reasons. Operations have been normal everywhere since morning. Workers at only two factories are observing work stoppages. No disorder has been reported elsewhere," he said.
He said the industrial zone has around 800 garment factories, of which approximately 30 remain closed.
Of these, 27 factories have been closed under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, four are observing general holidays, and nine have been declared closed indefinitely. Workers at two factories joined work but later stopped working, he added.
He said factory owners and other stakeholders all want stability in the garment sector.
Khairul Mamun Mintu, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Sweater Workers Trade Union Centre, said the situation had remained normal since morning.
"Some factories that were previously closed have reopened. Workers have joined work, and the situation remains normal so far. In a small number of factories where workers had joined but were not working, holidays have been declared under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act, following the 'no work, no pay' principle. Apart from these, the situation across the industrial zone is normal," he said.

item.title: Iran rules out UN inspections of damaged nuclear sites until war ends
item.description:
Iran will not let UN inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the Middle East war has ended and the United States meets its conditions, a senior Iranian official said.
The remarks came days after the International Atomic Energy Agency urged Tehran to take steps towards resuming inspections, which have been suspended since last year’s 12-day war with Israel, when the US also struck Iranian nuclear sites.
“We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran’s conditions are met and the war has permanently ended,” Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised interview late Sunday.
Iranian nuclear facilities were hit again during the Middle East war which broke out on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
IAEA inspectors visited Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant in September but have not gained access to other bombed sites including Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan.
Gharibabadi said the agency’s request to inspect damaged facilities was “likely aimed at assessing the effectiveness of American weaponry.”
Efforts to end the Middle East war have made little headway. Tehran is demanding that Washington unfreeze Iranian assets and lift sanctions, among other conditions, in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the vital energy shipping route it has blockaded during the conflict.
Iranian officials have said talks on Iran’s nuclear program would come at a later stage.
Earlier this month, the US military announced a $20 million reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program, a move Tehran called “repugnant.”

item.title: Bangladesh exports fruits worth $126.35m in FY26
item.description:
Bangladesh exported fruits worth $126.35 million in FY26, Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir told the parliament on Sunday.
“Bangladesh exports fruits to various international markets, including the United Arab Emirates, Austria, Australia, Bahrain, Canada, China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and the United States,” he said.
The minister said this while responding to a starred question from treasury bench member Md. Sadique Reaz (Dinajpur-2) during the day’s question-answer session in the House today with Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal in the chair.
The minister said Bangladesh currently exports fruits to various countries and territories, including Austria, Bahrain, Germany, Denmark, France, Greece, Hong Kong, Ireland, Italy, Kuwait, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Oman, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, Sweden, Singapore and Vietnam.
Muktadir outlined several initiatives undertaken by the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) to expand exports of mangoes and other agricultural products.
He said the EPB organized a seminar titled “Export Opportunities and Diversification of Mango and Mango Products” in Chapainawabganj on October 19, 2023, to explore export potential, market expansion and diversification of mango and mango-based products.
The EPB also held a view exchange meeting with local mango growers, exporters and other stakeholders in Chapainawabganj on May 20, 2025, in presence of its vice-chairman, he added.
The minister said the EPB had provided comprehensive assistance to exporters in completing the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) registration process to expand agricultural exports, particularly mango shipments, to China.
“Meridian Agro Industries Ltd. of Chattogram has secured GACC registration with the overall support of the Export Promotion Bureau,” he said.
He added that the EPB had also processed questionnaires submitted by Safe International Corporation and MTB Agro and Garden and forwarded them to the Commercial Counsellor at the Bangladesh Embassy in China on June 7, 2023.
Muktadir said the EPB vice-chairman inspected the Vapour Heat Treatment Plant in Gabtoli, Dhaka, on July 22, 2026, to assess the infrastructure and procedures required for agricultural exports.
An EPB meeting with all stakeholders was also held on August 10, 2026, to discuss exports of mangoes, jackfruits and other agricultural products to China and other international markets, GACC registration and ways to address existing barriers.
The minister said the EPB had taken initiatives to organize training programs involving the Department of Agricultural Extension, all stakeholders and exporters on GACC registration and registration procedures in other countries, phytosanitary requirements and export compliance.
The EPB also organized a training program for mango growers, farmers and stakeholders in Lama, Bandarban, on May 9, 2026.
The program covered mango production, disease and pest management, timely harvesting, grading and packaging, post-harvest management, vapour and hot water treatment, export procedures and marketing, he said.
The minister further said the EPB had undertaken a survey to assess the export potential of the country’s Geographical Indication (GI) products.
The survey will identify production capacity, product quality, international market demand, existing barriers, compliance requirements and potential export destinations for promising GI products. The EPB has finalised the terms of reference for appointing a survey firm, he added.
As part of efforts to promote and brand GI products and other promising agricultural goods in international markets, the EPB has included participation in six international trade fairs in its calendar for FY27.
The fairs include the 2026 Mekong-Lancang Fruits Festival in China’s Yunnan Province, the 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS) 2026, D-8 Halal Expo Indonesia 2026, Agro Food Jeddah 2026, the International Food and Drink Event and the International Halal Expo and World Halal Summit 2026.
The minister said these initiatives aimed to diversify agricultural exports, improve compliance with international standards and strengthen Bangladesh’s presence in global markets.

item.title: Pallabi child rape-murder: Swapna helped Sohel out of fear, prosecution tells HC
item.description:
The wife of Sohel Rana, who was sentenced to death for the rape and murder of an eight-year-old child Pallabi, was so afraid of her husband that she helped him in the killing, the prosecution told the High Court on Monday.
The submission came during the hearing on the death references and appeals filed by Sohel and his wife, Swapna Akter, before a High Court bench led by Justice Bhishmadev Chakrabortty.
The prosecution concluded its arguments on the day. Deputy Attorney General Barrister Mohammad Osman Chowdhury represented the state.
According to the case documents, the child's father lived with his family in a rented flat in Pallabi. He worked at a private office in Banani.
Sohel Rana and Swapna Akter lived in another flat in the same building. The child was a second-grade student at a local school.
On May 19, the child was raped and murdered. Sohel later escaped by cutting through the window grille of the room.
Police took Swapna into custody after receiving information through the national emergency helpline 999. Sohel was later arrested in front of Fatullah police station in Narayanganj.
The child's father filed a case with Pallabi police station over the incident. On May 21, Sohel gave a confessional statement before a court under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Both accused were subsequently sent to jail.
On May 25, the investigating officer, Sub-Inspector Ahiduzzaman of Pallabi police station, submitted a charge sheet against Sohel and Swapna. The case was sent to the tribunal for trial on the same day.
The trial began on June 1 with the framing of charges against the two accused. The following day, the prosecution presented 16 witnesses, completing the recording of testimony in a single day.
The accused were examined under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, on June 3.
On June 7, Judge Masrur Salequin of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children's Violence Suppression Tribunal sentenced both accused to death.
The tribunal also fined Sohel Tk5 lakh and Swapna Tk2 lakh, directing that the money be paid to the child's legal heirs.
The verdict was delivered just 19 days after the murder.
The death references containing the case records were subsequently sent to the High Court for confirmation of the sentences. Both convicts later filed jail appeals before the High Court.

item.title: Prime Bank signs MoU with BEPZA Public School and College
item.description:

Representing Bepza Public School and College were Major Md Anwarul Kabir (retd), principal, and Mohammad Nuruzzaman, director (accounts), Bepza KEPZ Zone .
Prime Bank continues to strengthen its engagement with educational institutions across Bangladesh, offering integrated financial solutions that support institutional efficiency and promote a culture of savings and financial awareness among the next generation.

item.title: SahajMobile secures up to $25m for smartphone financing
item.description:
SahajMobile has closed a credit facility with ALMA, enabling total borrowings of up to $25 million through its US holding company, HR Consortium USA, Inc.
Part of its broader Series A financing led by Beacon Peak Partners, the facility will support smartphone financing for underserved customers across Bangladesh.
Since launching in 2024, SahajMobile has helped tens of thousands of customers access smartphones through installment financing via more than 3,300 retail partners.
Combining proprietary technology, international credit expertise and local operations, it aims to finance one million customers by 2027, expanding connectivity and financial inclusion, particularly for women and rural communities.
Bangladesh’s credit and connectivity gaps remain substantial.
In 2024, approximately 16 million adults borrowed from formal sources, while roughly 76 million—62% of adults—did not own a personal smartphone.
Smartphone shipments reached 10.6 million units in 2025, up 22% year on year, underscoring demand for devices that connect people to the digital economy.
“There is an enormous credit story in this region that deserves more attention from institutional investors,” said Rafsun Faiz, founder and CEO of SahajMobile.
“We see an underserved market with real demand for credit. This financing will help us continue our growth and connect global capital with everyday borrowers across Bangladesh, starting with smartphone financing.”
SahajMobile’s management team brings lending, credit and technology experience from Guggenheim Partners, BAWAG, Google, Qualia, Macquarie, BlackRock and Kiavi, alongside local entrepreneurship and operating experience through co-founder and managing director Abu Al Motalib.
The team applies institutional underwriting, structuring and portfolio management to a market whose customers and operating conditions it knows firsthand.
Its proprietary technology supports financing across multiple smartphone brands and retail channels.
By combining capital, credit assessment and local distribution, SahajMobile makes installment financing accessible while maintaining responsible lending practices.
SahajMobile BD Ltd. has also received a No Objection Certificate from Bangladesh Bank.
The pilot prioritizes low-income people without smartphones and underserved areas approved by Bangladesh Bank, subject to operating conditions and ongoing monitoring.
“Digitizing Bangladesh starts with getting people connected,” said Abu Al Motalib, co-founder and managing director of SahajMobile.
“For someone in a rural community, a smartphone can be a tool to find work, reach customers, receive payments and access essential services. We want to make financing available for an asset that can help people earn, including women, who remain extremely underserved in the market.”

item.title: Adcelerate brings AI-powered ad campaign for Honor 600S 5G
item.description:
What if an advertisement could do more than show people what technology can do? What if they could experience it themselves?
Adcelerete Technologies Limited has introduced an interactive digital advertising campaign for the Honor 600S 5G, bringing an AI-powered image-to-video experience directly to audiences through the web.
The campaign features two advertising formats: an interactive floating experience and an image overlay placement within a digital news portal environment.
Both formats bring the Honor campaign into everyday digital browsing, offering audiences an opportunity to explore its creative concept through direct interaction.
At the centre of the floating experience is a browser-based image-to-video interface. Users can upload an image from their gallery or camera, enter a creative prompt and choose between portrait (9:16) and landscape (16:9) video formats.
The interface also includes an optional start-frame input. Users can generate a five-second video, preview the result and download their creation.
The image overlay format complements this experience by presenting the Honor creative within a news-style web portal environment, introducing the campaign alongside the content audiences are already browsing.
The campaign draws on the creative proposition of the Honor 600S 5G, which features AI Image to Video 2.0.
The feature is designed to help users turn images into video content through generative AI.
Its availability and service terms are subject to regional conditions and software updates.
Through this campaign, Adcelerete combines interactive media placements with an AI-led creative experience, giving the brand a way to demonstrate its product proposition beyond conventional display advertising.
It also reflects the growing opportunity for brands to use interactive formats to make technology-led campaigns more tangible and engaging.
The campaign marks another step in Adcelerete’s exploration of advertising formats that connect brand communication with audience experience.
